GRAMMAR WORDS: max-neg, very-neg, minor-neg, neutral, minor-pos, very-pos, max-pos
NOTES: These are can be used as modifiers for axis words

NOTES
Partial domains reuse a restricted subset of the root word space. Maybe 64, maybe 128 roots
This uses the entire restricted domain, but most people don't use base 64/128 numbers

Among other things, is very useful for numbers:

Can be used for something like "billions", "tenths", etc. Using numbers without using magnitudes is just rattling off digits which becomes very difficult to understand if it isn't known from context the magnitude of the numbers.

Magnitude uses the number domain. And it is agnostic to base.
When used with numbers, it plays a role similar to a part of scientific notation.

Consider 2e3, which is a 2 followed by 3 zeros, or 2000.
So to say this number in base 10, we would say something like:
"finger number 2 magnitude 3"

In base 10, "magnitude 3" would be like saying "thousands". One need not specify magnitude after every digit. In base 10, it might be great to specify magnitude at every 3 magnitudes, like "billions", "millions", and "thousands".

More examples:

2004 base 10 would be:
"finger number 2 magnitude 3 4 magnitude 0"
OR
"finger number 2 magnitude 3 0 0 4"

34,103,487 would be:
"finger number 3 4 magnitude 6 1 0 3 magnitude 3 4 8 7"

Magnitude can also be used to specify percents and decimal numbers:

23% would be:
"finger number 2 3 magnitude negative 2"

3 tenths would be:
"finger number 3 magnitude negative 1"

Note that unlike the number domain specifiers, the magnitude domain specifier can only be followed by one argument. Typically, that is going to be 1 root word in the restricted domain. If you need more than 64/128 magnitudes, then you can use a subclause with a number:

3e139 would be:
"finger number 3 magnitude which finger number 1 3 9 end-which"

Magnitude, when used with numbers is base agnostic. So, while in base 10, "magnitude 3" would be like saying "thousands", in base 2, "magnitude 3" would be "eights". And the convention about when to explicitly say magnitude might be different depending on base. In base 2, it might make sense to explicitly state magnitude at every 4 magnitudes ("sixteens").
